content.text: PHP is old, but the PHP you'd learn today isn't: it ships a new version every year, with types, enums and readonly properties, and Laravel 13 brings queues, testing and starter kits for Vue and Livewire. The outdated part is the pile of old tutorials. This roadmap takes you from zero to senior in five stages, with a project, the books and the official docs for each.
A student builds a final-year project from a popular PHP video course recorded a decade ago. The first

. A forum answer swaps in another function, the student keeps gluing form fields into the SQL string the way the course did, and the project ships with an SQL injection hole. The lesson they take away is that PHP is a relic. The real problem was the year of the course: Laravel's query builder
by default, and the student never got that far.
The belief: PHP is an old language for small sites, so learning Laravel today means learning outdated practices.

There's a reason people say it. PHP has been around for decades, a lot of legacy code is written in it, and search results still surface tutorials written for PHP 5. If that's all you've seen, "outdated" is a fair summary of what you saw.
The language moved on. PHP releases a new branch every year,
for two years of bug fixes and two more of security fixes, and released PHP 8.6 on 19 November 2026. Modern PHP code uses strict types, enums,

, readonly properties and property hooks. Laravel ships a major version every year; version 13 came out in March 2026, and its starter kits set up Vue with Inertia 3, Vue's Composition API, TypeScript and Tailwind. What's outdated is old learning material, so the skill is picking current sources.
What a Laravel full-stack developer really does

Most days you add features to an existing application: a route and a controller, an Eloquent model and its migration, a form request that validates input, a policy that decides who may do what, and a page in Blade, Vue or Livewire. Slow work such as sending emails or building exports goes into queued jobs, and every feature gets tests. You also deploy, keep queue workers and scheduled tasks running, upgrade Laravel once a year, and often maintain older code that predates the current conventions.

Two front-end routes are common. Inertia keeps Laravel's routing and controllers and renders Vue pages, so you don't build a separate JSON API. Livewire builds reactive components in PHP, which the Laravel docs describe as a good fit for teams that mostly use Blade.
The stages from zero to senior

This roadmap applies to Laravel 13 on PHP 8.5 (Laravel 13 supports PHP 8.3 to 8.5; check its support table before moving to 8.6), Vue 3.5 with Inertia 3 or Livewire 4, and MySQL 8.4 or 9.7, as of November 2026. Durations assume about 10 hours a week; at 20 hours, expect roughly half.

blocks.title: Pick Inertia or Livewire by your team

content.text: If you want a frontend skill you can carry to other stacks, take the Vue starter kit with Inertia. If your team writes mostly Blade and PHP, Livewire keeps you in one language. Learn one well before trying the other.

Put the app on GitHub with a README, seeders that fill it with demo data, and one command to run it. Let CI run your Pest or PHPUnit tests on every push, and deploy a live demo with a working queue.
